description: Local produce calendar by US state: months when each item is in season locally (harvest or local availability), from state agriculture department and Cooperative Extension charts, plus the USDA SNAP-Ed guide as a national block. Items are keyed by foods.json foodId where a food matches; otherwise foodId is null and name is the chart's name.
notWalmartAvailability: In-season local produce is not necessarily what Walmart (or any store) stocks: supermarkets source nationally and internationally year-round. Store availability lives only in each food's separate availability field (e.g. availability['walmart|lake-city|sc']) in foods.json/meals.json/grocery-lists.json; this file never states or implies store stock, and the two must not be mixed.

itemShape.name: name as printed on the chart
itemShape.months: sorted month numbers 1-12 (null only in the national block, which gives seasons)
itemShape.sourceName: matches a sources[].sourceName in the same block
itemShape.confidence: high = clearly marked on the chart; medium = partial-month bars or 'limited' months; low = not used

confidenceNote: Confidence describes how clearly the month is marked on the source chart, not the strength of any health claim.

user.note: The user stated zone 7b. The 2023 USDA map's ZIP lookup data (PRISM/Oregon State, via phzmapi.org) gives 8b for ZIP 29560 (Lake City, SC; 15 to 20 F). The SC state map shows 7b only in the cooler Upstate. Zones do not change the season windows below, which come from the state harvest charts.

hardinessZones.source: USDA Agricultural Research Service and Oregon State University PRISM Climate Group, 2023 USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map
hardinessZones.SCNote: Zones shown in the legend of the official 2023 South Carolina state map (7b in the Upstate to 9a/9b along the southern coast).

zip29560.source: phzmapi.org/29560.json (a public mirror of the 2023 PRISM zone data; the official lookup is the ZIP search at planthardiness.ars.usda.gov)

hardinessZones.meaning: Hardiness zones reflect the average annual extreme minimum winter temperature (1991-2020); they are not harvest timing. Season windows come from the harvest/availability charts.

why.summary: Seasonal or local produce is not proven to be healthier: fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables all count toward DGA servings, and reviews find frozen and canned produce nutritionally comparable to fresh for many nutrients. In-season produce is often cheaper because supply is abundant: USDA ERS found fresh vegetable prices vary through the year, most for corn and other starchy vegetables (lowest in summer, when availability peaks) and least for dark green vegetables. Use the calendar for price and taste, not as a health rule.

sources.title: Byrne AT, Sweitzer M. Starchy fresh vegetables (excluding potatoes) had the most seasonal price variation from 2016-18. USDA ERS Charts of Note, 2024-05-14.
Rickman JC, Barrett DM, Bruhn CM. Nutritional comparison of fresh, frozen and canned fruits and vegetables. Part 1. J Sci Food Agric. 2007;87(6):930-944.
USDA SNAP-Ed Seasonal Produce Guide ('fresh, frozen, canned, and dried: fruits and vegetables are a delicious way to make every bite count')

zipToState.source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 ZCTA to County Relationship File (tab20_zcta520_county20_natl.txt)
zipToState.method: Each 5-digit ZCTA's land area is split across counties; the county's state FIPS gives the state. For each 3-digit prefix, the state with the most ZCTA land area is the value; states holding at least 1% of the prefix's land area are listed in alsoStates (the value is then an object).
caveats: ZCTAs approximate USPS ZIP Codes: PO-box-only, unique (single-organization) and military ZIPs have no ZCTA, so their prefixes (e.g. 005, 090-099 APO/FPO) are missing. Fall back to asking the user's state.

USPS L002 3-Digit ZIP Code Prefix Matrix (https://postalpro.usps.com/node/2586) was checked but not used: its labels name the mail-processing facility, which can be in another state (e.g. prefixes 010-012, in Massachusetts, are labeled HARTFORD CT).

sources.title: South Carolina Produce Harvest Finder 2026 (Certified SC Grown)
sources.publisher: South Carolina Department of Agriculture, Certified SC Grown
sources.method: Month-by-month lists; each list was assigned to the month label printed beside it on the flyer. 'Always in season' (hydroponic produce, local milk, meat, fish, eggs, honey, cheeses) is not itemized.
ambiguityNotes: Tomatoes are not listed in the August block (as printed), though they are listed in June, July, September and October.
'Peas' (Sep-Nov) and 'Peas (Snap/Sugar)' (Apr-Aug) are listed separately; the flyer does not say what 'Peas' means.
'Squash (Variety)', 'Squash (Yellow/Winter)' and 'Summer Squash' are listed as printed.
'Mushrooms', 'Microgreens' and hydroponic produce are largely grown indoors.

sources.sourceName: SCDA South Carolina Produce Availability chart (2019)
sources.title: South Carolina Produce Availability (chart)
sources.method: Dot chart; dots detected from a 110-dpi render of the PDF and assigned to the 12 month columns and 32 printed rows (181 dots).
ambiguityNotes: Older (2019) chart; where it differs from the 2026 Harvest Finder, prefer the 2026 flyer.
Several rows are categories (Leafy Greens, Oriental Vegetables).

sources.title: Planning a Garden (HGIC 1256, Table 1: planting dates by region) and Seasonal Fruit/Veggies in South Carolina
sources.publisher: Clemson Cooperative Extension, Home & Garden Information Center
sources.method: Not used for months. Clemson publishes planting dates (Coastal Plain vs Piedmont) and days to maturity, not a harvest calendar; turning planting dates into harvest months would be an estimate. Its 'Seasonal Fruit/Veggies in South Carolina' page (https://hgic.clemson.edu/seasonal-fruit-veggies-in-south-carolina/) reproduces a PickYourOwn.org chart, a commercial site, so it is not used either.
sources.regionNote: Clemson places Florence County (Lake City, ZIP 29560) in the Coastal Plain gardening region.
